question: Refer to the exhibit. A Cisco data center environment is implemented with vPC. The web server replies using the SVI MAC address as the Layer 2 header instead of the HSRP MAC address on VLAN 23. This behavior causes packet drops on the Cisco Nexus 9000 Series Switches due to the vPC loop prevention mechanism. The requirement is for the vPC feature to allow N9K_1 and N9K_2 to forward traffic between the NAS server and the web server, even if the HSRP's MAC address is not used on Layer 2 headers for VLAN 23. Which feature must be used to accomplish this goal?
context: Topology: NAS (Vlan 23, 192.168.23.0/24) - N9K_3 - vPC 23/Port-Channel 23 - N9K_1/N9K_2 (HSRP MAC 00c1.BEEF.CAFE.0023 for Vlan23, 00c1.BEEF.CAFE.0012 for Vlan12) - vPC 12/Port-Channel 12 - Web Server (Vlan 12, 192.168.12.0/24).
imageNote: Diagram: NAS (Vlan23) connects to N9K_3, which connects via vPC 23/Port-Channel 23 to N9K_1/N9K_2 (HSRP MAC 00c1.BEEF.CAFE.0023 for Vlan23, 00c1.BEEF.CAFE.0012 for Vlan12); N9K_1/N9K_2 connect via vPC 12/Port-Channel 12 to Web Server (Vlan12).
theory: Normally a vPC peer only routes traffic destined to the shared HSRP virtual MAC address; if a downstream device replies using the SVI's own burned-in MAC address instead, port-channel hashing might deliver that frame to the vPC peer that doesn't own that MAC, and vPC's duplicate-frame-prevention rule then blocks the frame from exiting toward its destination because it arrived over the peer link. The vPC peer-gateway feature fixes this by letting each vPC peer also locally route frames addressed to its peer's burned-in MAC, so traffic never needs to cross the peer link at all regardless of which gateway MAC the sending host used. (CCNP/CCIE DCCOR Official Cert Guide, Chapter 2 — vPC Peer Gateway)
